climate: Seasons this cool ripen Pinot Gris, Müller-Thurgau, Gewürztraminer and Riesling fully without cooking off their freshness.
Pinot Gris sits in its sweet spot, so the wines can show the style it is known for.
Pinot Noir is at its cool limit. In cool years it can stay underripe, with green, sharp flavors.
Chardonnay is at its cool limit. In cool years it can stay underripe, with green, sharp flavors.
Most rain falls in winter. Dry summers keep mildew and rot down, though young vines may need watering.

soil.rock: Clay holds water well but drains poorly. It stays cool, which slows ripening and keeps acidity up.
soil.top: The topsoil holds water well and drains at a steady pace, so vines rarely go thirsty or sit in wet ground. Its pH is close to neutral, so vines take up the nutrients they need easily.

land: The high ground runs about 3°F cooler than the low ground. Higher vineyards ripen later and keep more acidity, so one grape can make lighter or richer wine here depending on height.
Much of it is steep. Cold air and rain run off, so frost and waterlogging are rare and soils stay thin, keeping yields low. Steep rows are slow and costly to work, often by hand.
